items.title: The Soviet economy grew faster than the US for decades
items.claim: From the 1928 first Five-Year Plan to the late 1960s, how did Soviet growth compare to US growth?

options.text: The Soviet economy was always smaller and grew more slowly than the US
Soviet GDP growth averaged roughly 5-6% annually through the 1950s, faster than the US in the same period — before stagnating sharply in the 1970s-80s
Soviet GDP collapsed in 1932 and never recovered
The Soviet economy never produced reliable statistics

items.reveal:
CIA estimates put Soviet GDP growth at 5.7% (1950s) and 5.2% (1960s), against US rates of 3-4%. The growth was 'extensive' — pulling labour out of agriculture, building heavy industry, exploiting massive natural resources — rather than 'intensive' productivity gains.

By the 1970s the extensive sources were exhausted. Innovation faltered, oil propped up the system in the 1970s, then the 1980s collapse came when oil prices fell and reform under Gorbachev destabilised what remained.

Robert Allen, Stephen Kotkin and others have documented this trajectory in detail.
items.why: 'Communism never works' as a one-liner ignores 40 years of measurable, fast growth. The interesting question is why the model worked for extensive industrialisation but failed at the next stage.

items.title: The Great Moderation ended in 2008
items.claim: From roughly 1985 to 2007, US and UK output volatility fell substantially compared to earlier decades. What did Ben Bernanke call this period in 2004?

options.text: The Great Moderation — and Bernanke credited a combination of better monetary policy, structural changes (services, JIT) and good luck. The period ended emphatically with the 2008 crisis

items.reveal_title: Stability that turned out not to be
items.reveal:
Bernanke's 2004 speech 'The Great Moderation' attributed reduced volatility to improvements in policy. The 2008 crisis suggested 'good luck' had played a larger role than recognised.

Hyman Minsky's earlier 'financial instability hypothesis' argued that stable periods breed speculative behaviour that ultimately destabilises the system — the 'Minsky moment' became a widely used term after 2008.
items.why: Periods of low volatility can mask growing fragility. Confidence in macroeconomic stability before 2008 was substantial; the consensus was wrong.

items.title: Behavioural economics dismantled the rational agent
items.claim: Kahneman and Tversky's 1979 paper on Prospect Theory introduced a different model of choice. What's the key finding?

options.text: People are perfectly rational expected-utility maximisers
People weigh losses roughly twice as heavily as equivalent gains, and evaluate outcomes relative to a reference point rather than in absolute terms
People only care about wealth, never relative position
Rational choice perfectly predicts behaviour once information costs are included

items.reveal:
Prospect Theory (Kahneman & Tversky, Econometrica, 1979) replaced expected utility's smooth concave function with a kinked value function — steeper for losses than for gains — and replaced objective probabilities with subjective decision weights that overweight small probabilities.

Kahneman won the 2002 Nobel; Tversky had died in 1996 (the prize is not awarded posthumously). Richard Thaler extended the work into 'nudge' policy; Esther Duflo and others into development economics.

The homo economicus of textbook microeconomics still appears in models — but is now understood as an idealisation, not a description.
items.why: Microeconomics taught as if people are rational misrepresents both the discipline and the actual evidence. The behavioural turn is one of the most important shifts in economics in 50 years.
